The derived set of multiple star polylogarithms

Jiangtao Li Email address: lijiangtao@csu.edu.cn Address: Jiangtao Li
School of Mathematics and Statistics, HNP-LAMA, Central South University, Hunan Province, China
Abstract.

The derived set of multiple zeta-star values is the half-line [1,+∞)[1,+\infty). In this paper we study the corresponding two-dimensional problem for multiple star polylogarithms on the unit circle. We first prove that every shifted multiple star polylogarithm is the generating function of a completely monotone sequence and hence admits a normalized Hausdorff–Stieltjes representation. Both the shifted and the unshifted functions, as well as their infinite-depth limits, are shown to be univalent on the half-plane Re​z<1\mathrm{Re}\,z<1.

For finite indices, the representing densities satisfy a strict monotone likelihood-ratio order with respect to the reverse lexicographic order. Together with closure properties of the Hausdorff–Stieltjes class and a limiting quotient argument, this shows that, along the upper semicircle, the argument of each translated curve increases strictly while its modulus decreases strictly; the corresponding lower-semicircle statement follows by conjugation. The same idea gives strict separation of the curves attached to different indices. We then establish a one-to-one correspondence between a natural set of pairs consisting of a point of the unit circle and an infinite index, and the closed half-plane Re​w≥12\mathrm{Re}\,w\geq\frac{1}{2} with the point 11 removed. Under a binary coordinate on the index set, this correspondence is a homeomorphism.

As an application, a subclass of shifted cyclotomic multiple zeta-star values of all levels form a countable dense subset of the open half-plane Re​w>12\mathrm{Re}\,w>\frac{1}{2}. Consequently, the derived set, and every higher derived set, of this cyclotomic family is the closed half-plane Re​w≥12\mathrm{Re}\,w\geq\frac{1}{2}.

1. Introduction

Multiple zeta values and multiple zeta-star values are defined respectively by

ζ⁡(k1,…,kr)=∑n1>⋯>nr≥11n1k1⋯nrkr,\zeta(k_{1},\ldots,k_{r})=\sum_{n_{1}>\cdots>n_{r}\geq 1}\frac{1}{n_{1}^{k_{1}}\cdots n_{r}^{k_{r}}},
ζ⋆(k1,…,kr)=∑n1≥⋯≥nr≥11n1k1⋯nrkr,k1≥2,k2,…,kr≥1.\zeta^{\star}(k_{1},\ldots,k_{r})=\sum_{n_{1}\geq\cdots\geq n_{r}\geq 1}\frac{1}{n_{1}^{k_{1}}\cdots n_{r}^{k_{r}}},\qquad k_{1}\geq 2,\quad k_{2},\ldots,k_{r}\geq 1.

Their weight and depth are k1+⋯+krk_{1}+\cdots+k_{r} and rr, respectively. These values occur naturally in the study of iterated integrals, multiple series, mixed Tate motives, algebraic KK-theory; see, for example, [10, 3, 5, 2, 9, 11, 12, 17, 31]. They also arise in perturbative quantum field theory and in the evaluation of Feynman integrals; see [1, 6, 27]. In addition to their algebraic relations, it is natural to ask for the order, topology, and metric geometry of the sets formed by these special values.

Denote by 𝒵⋆\mathcal{Z}^{\star} the set of multiple zeta-star values. In [20], the author obtained a natural total order on 𝒵⋆\mathcal{Z}^{\star} from multiple integral representations. Denote by ℤ+\mathbb{Z}^{+} the set of positive integers. Define

𝒯={(k1,⋯,kr,…)∈(ℤ+)∞|k1≥2,(k1,⋯,kr,⋯)≠(2,{1}∞)}.\mathcal{T}=\bigg\{(k_{1},\cdots,k_{r},\ldots)\in(\mathbb{Z}^{+})^{\infty}\,\bigg|\,k_{1}\geq 2,(k_{1},\cdots,k_{r},\cdots)\neq(2,\{1\}^{\infty})\bigg\}.

Then the map

η:𝒯→(1,+∞),\eta:\mathcal{T}\rightarrow(1,+\infty),
(k1,⋯,kr,…)↦limr→+∞ζ⋆​(k1,…,kr)(k_{1},\cdots,k_{r},\ldots)\mapsto\lim_{r\rightarrow+\infty}\zeta^{\star}(k_{1},\ldots,k_{r})

is bijective. This is Theorem 1.3 of [20]. We call the map η\eta zeta-star correspondence. An equivalent correspondence was found independently by Hirose, Murahara and Onozuka in [15]. It implies that 𝒵⋆\mathcal{Z}^{\star} is dense in (1,+∞)(1,+\infty) and that its derived set is [1,+∞)[1,+\infty). The result may be compared with continued fractions: an infinite symbolic index provides a coordinate for an ordinary real interval. It has since led to rational deformations, Diophantine approximation and normalized approximation function, restricted sumsets and product sets, finite correspondences, and complex analytic variations [21, 22, 23, 24, 25]. Kamano [18] investigated the order structure of a class of multi- polylogarithm functions.

In the present paper this one-dimensional bijection is used only when both unit-circle parameters equal 11. For |z|<1|z|<1, the multiple polylogarithm and the multiple star polylogarithm are

Lik1,…,kr​(z)=∑n1>⋯>nr≥1zn1n1k1⋯nrkr,\mathrm{Li}_{k_{1},\ldots,k_{r}}(z)=\sum_{n_{1}>\cdots>n_{r}\geq 1}\frac{z^{n_{1}}}{n_{1}^{k_{1}}\cdots n_{r}^{k_{r}}},
Lik1,…,kr⋆​(z)=∑n1≥⋯≥nr≥1zn1n1k1⋯nrkr.\mathrm{Li}^{\star}_{k_{1},\ldots,k_{r}}(z)=\sum_{n_{1}\geq\cdots\geq n_{r}\geq 1}\frac{z^{n_{1}}}{n_{1}^{k_{1}}\cdots n_{r}^{k_{r}}}.

If k1≥2k_{1}\geq 2, these series are absolutely convergent on |z|=1|z|=1. If k1=1k_{1}=1 and |z|=1|z|=1, z≠1z\neq 1, their boundary values are defined by partial sums with respect to the outer variable n1n_{1}. Section 3 shows that these sums agree with the analytic continuations. Denote by

Li~k1,…,kr⋆​(z)=Lik1,…,kr⋆​(z)z.\widetilde{\mathrm{Li}}^{\star}_{k_{1},\ldots,k_{r}}(z)=\frac{\mathrm{Li}^{\star}_{k_{1},\ldots,k_{r}}(z)}{z}.

We call it the shifted multiple star polylogarithm.

Multiple polylogarithms (MPLs) constitute a broad family of multivalued transcendental functions that simultaneously generalize the classical polylogarithm Lin⁡(z)\operatorname{Li}_{n}(z) and multiple zeta values. Although they may be introduced through nested power series, their most flexible formulation is in terms of Chen iterated integrals of logarithmic differential forms on punctured projective lines. This representation makes their analytic continuation, differential equations, monodromy, and algebraic structure particularly transparent [3, 11]. MPLs are commonly organized by their weight and depth and satisfy rich systems of functional identities. In particular, the iterated-integral representation gives rise to shuffle relations, whereas the nested-series representation produces stuffle, or quasi-shuffle, relations; the compatibility of these two algebraic structures plays a central role in the study of multiple zeta values and their generalizations [8, 11, 12]. The p-adic iterated integration of MPLs is fundamental to the theory of p-adic multiple zeta values [4, 8]. Goncharov’s Hopf-algebraic and motivic formulation relates MPLs to periods of mixed Tate structures, motivic fundamental groups, and Galois actions, while Brown’s results demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework in describing the structure of motivic multiple zeta values [2, 11, 12]. Beyond arithmetic geometry and number theory, MPLs have become an essential function space in perturbative quantum field theory, since broad classes of multiloop Feynman integrals and scattering amplitudes can be expressed, simplified, and evaluated in terms of MPLs, their symbols, coproducts, and associated hyperlogarithmic integration algorithms [1, 6, 27]. These connections motivate continuing research on functional identities, bases and algebraic independence, special values, single-valued and motivic versions, analytic continuation, and efficient symbolic and numerical evaluation.

The passage from the real interval to the unit circle introduces a geometric function-theoretic problem. The coefficients of a shifted multiple star polylogarithm form a Hausdorff moment sequence. Thus the function belongs to the normalized Hausdorff–Stieltjes class

h⁡(z)=∫[0,1]d​μ​(t)1−t​z,μ⁡([0,1])=1.h(z)=\int_{[0,1]}\frac{d\mu(t)}{1-tz},\qquad\mu([0,1])=1.

This connects the subject with completely monotone sequences, Pick functions, and univalent functions; see [14, 29, 30, 7, 13]. A central point of the present paper is that the representing measures are not merely ordered: their densities satisfy a strict monotone likelihood-ratio order. This strictness is what prevents two different index curves from intersection on the unit circle.

𝒟={z∈ℂ|Rez<1},Λ=ℂ∖[1,+∞).\mathcal{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}\,|\,\mathrm{Re}\,z<1\},\qquad\Lambda=\mathbb{C}\setminus[1,+\infty).

Theorem 1.4.

The set 𝒞⋆\mathcal{C}^{\star} is a countable dense subset of ℋo\mathcal{H}^{o}. Consequently,

(𝒞⋆)(n)=ℋ,n≥1.(\mathcal{C}^{\star})^{(n)}=\mathcal{H},\qquad n\geq 1.

We call the bijective map η𝒮\eta_{\mathcal{S}} polylogarithms star correspondence. The polylogarithms star correspondence is a generalization of original zeta star correspondence. The correspondence has several potential applications. First, it gives a symbolic coordinate system for the punctured half-plane, in which the radial coordinate is encoded by an infinite positive-integer sequence and the angular coordinate is encoded by a point of the unit circle. Secondly, Theorem 1.4 provides a constructive approximation principle: every point of ℋo\mathcal{H}^{o} can be approximated by cyclotomic multiple zeta-star values. This may be useful in experimental arithmetic and in the numerical study of special values at roots of unity. Thirdly, the Hausdorff–Stieltjes representation gives positivity, moment inequalities, and Pick-function structure, which can be used for coefficient estimates and boundary-value problems. These applications are geometric and approximation-theoretic. The occurrence of the half-plane Re​w≥12\mathrm{Re}\,w\geq\frac{1}{2} by itself does not imply a statement about zeros of the Riemann zeta function.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 constructs the finite and infinite-depth functions and proves the special limiting identities needed later. Section 3 establishes complete monotonicity and univalence. Section 4 proves strict separation of unit-circle curves by the Hausdorff–Stieltjes and monotone likelihood-ratio method. Section 5 proves Theorem 1.2 by introducing the binary index coordinate and applying the invariance of domain theorem to a proper injective map. Section 6 proves the cyclotomic density and the derived-set statement.

The main results of this paper are inspired by the following beautiful formula

Let 𝐤=(k1,⋯,kr,…)∈𝒯^{\bf k}=(k_{1},\cdots,k_{r},\ldots)\in\widehat{\mathcal{T}}. By Lemma 2.1, (i​i​i)(iii), the limit

3. Completely monotone sequences and univalent functions

We now place the functions of Section 2 in the Hausdorff–Stieltjes class. Besides proving Theorem 1.1, the constructions in this section provide the representing densities used in the strict separation argument.

Definition 3.1.

Let Δ​xn=xn−xn+1\Delta x_{n}=x_{n}-x_{n+1}. A sequence {xn}n≥0\{x_{n}\}_{n\geq 0} of nonnegative real numbers is called completely monotone if

Δm​xn≥0,m,n≥0.\Delta^{m}x_{n}\geq 0,\qquad m,n\geq 0.

We recall the classical theorem of Hausdorff [14, 29].

Theorem 3.2 (Hausdorff).

A sequence {xn}n≥0\{x_{n}\}_{n\geq 0} is completely monotone if and only if there is a finite nonnegative Borel measure μ\mu on [0,1][0,1] such that

xn=∫[0,1]tn​𝑑μ​(t),n≥0.x_{n}=\int_{[0,1]}t^{n}\,d\mu(t),\qquad n\geq 0.

If x0=1x_{0}=1, then μ\mu is a probability measure.

For a nonnegative integrable function uu on (0,1)(0,1), define

(3.1) (𝖬​u)​(t)=∫t1u⁡(v)v​𝑑v,(𝖢​u)​(t)=∫0tu⁡(v)1−v​𝑑v.(\mathsf{M}u)(t)=\int_{t}^{1}\frac{u(v)}{v}\,dv,\qquad(\mathsf{C}u)(t)=\int_{0}^{t}\frac{u(v)}{1-v}\,dv.

Tonelli’s theorem gives, for every n≥0n\geq 0,

(3.2) ∫01tn​(𝖬​u)​(t)​𝑑t\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}t^{n}(\mathsf{M}u)(t)\,dt =1n+1​∫01tn​u​(t)​𝑑t,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n+1}\int_{0}^{1}t^{n}u(t)\,dt,
(3.3) ∫01tn​(𝖢​u)​(t)​𝑑t\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}t^{n}(\mathsf{C}u)(t)\,dt =1n+1​∑j=0n∫01tj​u​(t)​𝑑t.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n+1}\sum_{j=0}^{n}\int_{0}^{1}t^{j}u(t)\,dt.

Taking n=0n=0 shows that both operators preserve the total integral.

where no 𝖢\mathsf{C} occurs when r=1r=1, and composition is read from right to left. Here 𝟏{\bf 1} means the constant function 11 on [0,1][0,1]. Every such function is positive and locally absolutely continuous on (0,1)(0,1).

We shall use two standard results from geometric function theory. The first is due to Wirths [30].

Theorem 3.5 (Wirths).

If {xn}n≥0\{x_{n}\}_{n\geq 0} is completely monotone and x0=1x_{0}=1, then

(𝖢​u𝖢​v)′=v⁡(t)(1−t)​(𝖢​v)​(t)​(u⁡(t)v⁡(t)−(𝖢​u)​(t)(𝖢​v)​(t))≥0,\left(\frac{\mathsf{C}u}{\mathsf{C}v}\right)^{\prime}=\frac{v(t)}{(1-t)(\mathsf{C}v)(t)}\left(\frac{u(t)}{v(t)}-\frac{(\mathsf{C}u)(t)}{(\mathsf{C}v)(t)}\right)\geq 0,
(𝖬​u𝖬​v)′=v⁡(t)t​(𝖬​v)​(t)​((𝖬​u)​(t)(𝖬​v)​(t)−u⁡(t)v⁡(t))≥0.\left(\frac{\mathsf{M}u}{\mathsf{M}v}\right)^{\prime}=\frac{v(t)}{t(\mathsf{M}v)(t)}\left(\frac{(\mathsf{M}u)(t)}{(\mathsf{M}v)(t)}-\frac{u(t)}{v(t)}\right)\geq 0.

5. The polylogarithm-star correspondence

We now turn the separation theorem into a global parametrization of the half-plane. The radial parameter is supplied by the first moment.

6. Cyclotomic density and derived sets

We finish with the approximation consequence of the correspondence.

The set 𝒞⋆\mathcal{C}^{\star} is countable. We first show that it is contained in ℋo\mathcal{H}^{o}. For z∈S1∖{1}z\in S^{1}\setminus\{1\} and a finite index 𝐤{\bf k}, equations (3.6) and (5.5) give

because the density σ𝐤\sigma_{\bf k} is positive on (0,1)(0,1) and is not concentrated at 11. At z=1z=1, the convergence condition in the definition of 𝒞⋆\mathcal{C}^{\star} gives k1≥2k_{1}\geq 2, and

H𝐤​(1)=ζ⋆​(𝐤)>1.H_{\bf k}(1)=\zeta^{\star}({\bf k})>1.

Thus 𝒞⋆⊆ℋo\mathcal{C}^{\star}\subseteq\mathcal{H}^{o}.

Let w∈ℋo∖{1}w\in\mathcal{H}^{o}\setminus\{1\}. By Theorem 1.2, there is a unique pair (z,𝐤)∈𝒮​𝒯~(z,{\bf k})\in\widetilde{\mathcal{ST}} such that

w=H𝐤​(z).w=H_{\bf k}(z).

If z≠1z\neq 1, choose roots of unity zr≠1z_{r}\neq 1 tending to zz and let 𝐤(r)=(k1,…,kr){\bf k}^{(r)}=(k_{1},\ldots,k_{r}). Choose a closed arc K⊂S1∖{1}K\subset S^{1}\setminus\{1\} containing zz and all sufficiently large zrz_{r}; then KK is a compact subset of 𝒟\mathcal{D}. Lemma 4.10 and continuity of H𝐤H_{\bf k} give

|H𝐤(r)​(zr)−H𝐤​(z)|≤supζ∈K|H𝐤(r)​(ζ)−H𝐤​(ζ)|+|H𝐤​(zr)−H𝐤​(z)|→0.\begin{split}|H_{{\bf k}^{(r)}}(z_{r})-H_{\bf k}(z)|&\leq\sup_{\zeta\in K}|H_{{\bf k}^{(r)}}(\zeta)-H_{\bf k}(\zeta)|+|H_{\bf k}(z_{r})-H_{\bf k}(z)|\rightarrow 0.\end{split}

Every term on the left belongs to 𝒞⋆\mathcal{C}^{\star}. If z=1z=1, then 𝐤∈𝒯{\bf k}\in\mathcal{T} and, by the definition of the infinite zeta-star value,

H(k1,…,kr)​(1)=ζ⋆​(k1,…,kr)→H𝐤​(1)=w.H_{(k_{1},\ldots,k_{r})}(1)=\zeta^{\star}(k_{1},\ldots,k_{r})\rightarrow H_{\bf k}(1)=w.

Finally, the omitted point 11 is also a limit point, because

H(q)​(−1)=∑m=1+∞(−1)m−1mq→1(q→+∞).H_{(q)}(-1)=\sum_{m=1}^{+\infty}\frac{(-1)^{m-1}}{m^{q}}\rightarrow 1\qquad(q\rightarrow+\infty).

Hence 𝒞⋆\mathcal{C}^{\star} is dense in ℋo\mathcal{H}^{o}.

Since 𝒞⋆⊆ℋo\mathcal{C}^{\star}\subseteq\mathcal{H}^{o} and ℋo¯=ℋ\overline{\mathcal{H}^{o}}=\mathcal{H}, one has (𝒞⋆)′⊆ℋ(\mathcal{C}^{\star})^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{H}. Conversely, every neighborhood of a point of ℋ\mathcal{H} contains a nonempty open subset VV of ℋo\mathcal{H}^{o}. The dense set 𝒞⋆\mathcal{C}^{\star} meets VV infinitely often: otherwise, deleting the finitely many points of V∩𝒞⋆V\cap\mathcal{C}^{\star} would leave a nonempty open subset of VV disjoint from 𝒞⋆\mathcal{C}^{\star}. Thus every point of ℋ\mathcal{H} is an accumulation point, and

(𝒞⋆)′=ℋ.(\mathcal{C}^{\star})^{\prime}=\mathcal{H}.

The closed half-plane has no isolated points, so ℋ′=ℋ\mathcal{H}^{\prime}=\mathcal{H}. Induction gives

(𝒞⋆)(n)=ℋ,n≥1.(\mathcal{C}^{\star})^{(n)}=\mathcal{H},\qquad n\geq 1.

This proves the theorem. ∎

Remark 6.1.

The proof is constructive in the following sense. Once the inverse image (z,𝐤)(z,{\bf k}) of a target point has been found, truncating 𝐤{\bf k} and replacing zz by nearby roots of unity produces an explicit sequence of cyclotomic multiple zeta-star values.
